smm_pool.text: Key takeaways YouTube pays per ad view, not per video view, typically an estimated $5 to $15 per 1,000 ad views in 2026. Your earnings per view depend on your content niche, audience location, ad type, video length, and seasonal advertiser demand. RPM (revenue per mille) shows what you actually earn after YouTube’s 45% cut, while CPM reflects what advertisers pay. Ad revenue is only one income stream. Brand deals, channel memberships, affiliate marketing, and merch can meaningfully increase total YouTube earnings. How YouTube’s pay-per-view system works YouTube does have a pay-per-view system , but it might not be what you’d initially think. Instead of getting paid for each video view, YouTubers are paid for each ad view. Let’s dig a little deeper into what these two types of views mean: Video views: The number of views your video gets. Ad views: The number of views that ads on your video get. YouTube pays you for the amount of ad views your video gets. If your video has a million views but no advertising on it, you won’t be making any money. If your video has a million views but only 10,000 ad views, you’ll be making money only on the 10,000 ad views. Similarly, you might have multiple ads run within a single YouTube video. If users actually watch those ads all the way through, you could also end up with more ad views than video views. Essentially, YouTube makes money off the advertising space, so it will only pay based on how much exposure your video generates for that advertising space. Of that advertising money, YouTube keeps 45% and you keep 55% . Through this model, YouTube has paid creators over $100 billion since 2021. The short version: Your YouTube income is a share of ad revenue tied to ad views, not a flat rate per video view. Loyal customers cost less to retain than new ones cost to acquire, spend more over time, and actively recommend the brand to others. Building brand loyalty in 2026 requires consistent experiences, personalized engagement, fast customer care, and smart use of AI to anticipate customer needs. Key metrics for tracking brand loyalty include net promoter score, customer lifetime value, engagement rate, and sentiment analysis. What is brand loyalty? Brand loyalty is the connection between a brand and a customer that drives someone to make repeat purchases from a specific brand. They stick with that brand even when alternative suppliers or products may be cheaper or more easily accessible. The lineup outside the Apple Store to get the latest iPhone the first morning it’s available? That’s brand loyalty in action. What separates loyalty from habit is the emotional connection behind the purchase. A habitual buyer picks your product because it’s there. A loyal customer picks it because it says something about who they are, and because they trust you to deliver. That trust is built over time through familiarity with your brand (also known as brand awareness ), satisfying early experiences, and consistency after the sale. smm_pool.title: How to Increase Your LinkedIn Followers — What I've Learned From 25K of My Own and Millions of Posts of Buffer Data
smm_pool.text: LinkedIn is still one of the best places to build an audience from scratch, and you can increase your LinkedIn followers there organically, with no paid ads, no follower buying, and no growth hacks. When I went through 52 million posts across 10 platforms for our State of Social Media Engagement report , LinkedIn had the highest median engagement rate of any platform we looked at, at around 6.2%. LinkedIn has also become the most-cited website in AI search for professional questions, according to Profound's tracking, and more of what gets cited is what people post. So what you share on LinkedIn can show up when someone asks ChatGPT about your field. It's worked for me, too. I made my account in 2017 but only started posting in 2020 , when I was looking for community after losing my job. I now have over 25,000 followers, and posting has led to brand partnerships and invites onto podcasts and YouTube channels, which I never would've thought possible when I started. You don't need millions of followers, and you don't need to be the world's foremost expert in your niche. A smaller following that cares about what you have to say will do far more for you than a huge one that doesn't. So if you really, really want to grow on LinkedIn, whether as a creator, a founder, a business owner, or someone starting from zero, this guide is for you. It pairs what's worked for me with Buffer's data on millions of LinkedIn posts, and there's a section for company pages too. Key takeaways Switch your profile's main button from Connect to Follow. Connections are capped at 30,000 and need a yes from both sides, while followers have no cap, and everyone who connects with you follows you anyway. Stick to three to five topics. LinkedIn's feed now matches posts to people based on what they're about, so a clear focus helps it find your audience. Try carousels. In Buffer's analysis of 52 million posts, LinkedIn carousels had a median engagement rate of 21.77%, about three times video and nearly seven times text-only posts. Don't worry about posting too often. In Buffer's study of 2 million+ LinkedIn posts, accounts posting 11 or more times a week averaged nearly 17,000 more impressions per post. Reply to your comments. About 83% of LinkedIn profiles in Buffer's data performed better when they replied, the highest share of any platform. Keep your posts sounding like you. LinkedIn added a "Seems like AI slop" report option in July 2026, and flagged posts are seeing about 40% fewer views.
